passage: The report was due at nine the next morning, and the cleaners' vacuum roared outside the glass door. Omkar's manager Pranav had left one line at the top of the file: "Not good enough." No example, no reason. Omkar read it four times. He messaged, "Which section?" and an hour later the reply came: "Overall." He felt stung, then stuck, with no idea where to begin. Near midnight he rewrote every page, changing charts and headings that may have been fine. In the morning Pranav skimmed the new version, said "Better," and went into a meeting. Omkar sat at his desk, no wiser about what had been wrong.

qa.q: What did Pranav write at the top of the report?
qa.a: Pranav wrote "Not good enough." with no example and no reason.

qa.q: What was Omkar feeling after reading the comment four times?
qa.a: Omkar felt stung and lost, because the comment hurt but gave him nothing to act on.

qa.q: What could Omkar ask Pranav to make the feedback usable?
qa.a: He could ask Pranav for one concrete spot that fell short and what better would look like there, ideally in a short talk instead of a message.

qa.q: How might Pranav see this review?
qa.a: Pranav may think a quick line is efficient when busy, without realising the comment left Omkar guessing and rewriting everything. 🤔

grounding: Shows a worker receiving a vague verdict with no example, feeling stung and lost and unable to act on it.

passage: Vishal, the senior editor, stopped at Payal's desk in the Bengaluru office with a printout of her brochure copy. "It's just not working. Make it sharper." "Which lines?" Payal asked. "Overall. You'll get it," he said, and took a call. She spent Tuesday swapping adjectives and rewrote the headline three times. On Wednesday he glanced at it in passing. "Still not it." Her eyes prickled. She said "Okay" brightly and walked to the pantry, where her tea had gone cold on the shelf. Back at her desk she opened a blank page and stared at it, more lost than on Monday.

qa.q: Where did Vishal stop with the printout?
qa.a: Vishal stopped at Payal's desk in the Bengaluru office.

qa.q: What was Payal feeling when she said "Okay" brightly on Wednesday?
qa.a: Payal was hurt and covering it, since her eyes prickled and she went to the pantry instead of showing it.

qa.q: What could Payal try to get useful feedback from Vishal?
qa.a: She could bring two versions and ask which line in each felt weakest and why, so the answer has to be specific.

qa.q: What would change for Payal if Vishal had pointed to one paragraph?
qa.a: She would know where to work and what to fix, and the comment would inform her instead of only stinging.

grounding: Shows a worker receiving vague comments with no example, feeling both stung and lost.

passage: Vasudha, twenty-four, had worked two weeks on the product brochure at the Bengaluru start-up. On Friday her manager Zubin returned it with one line scrawled across the cover: "Not good enough. Redo." No marks inside. No example. She sat at her desk, face hot, flipping through the pages. Was it the photos? The tone? The layout? She'd followed the brief. On the metro home she replayed it, feeling stung and completely lost. That night she wrote to him: "Could you point to two or three places that need to change, and what good would look like?" On Monday he circled the headline and the price table. "These," he said. "Make them shorter." It took her an hour.

qa.q: What did Zubin write on the brochure's cover?
qa.a: "Not good enough. Redo."

qa.q: How did Vasudha feel on the metro home?
qa.a: She felt stung and completely lost, unsure what to change because there were no specifics.

qa.q: What did Vasudha do that turned the vague comment into useful feedback?
qa.a: She politely asked Zubin to point to two or three places and describe what good would look like.

qa.q: How might Zubin see his one-line comment after circling the two parts?
qa.a: Zubin might realise that the fix was small and specific, and that his vague note had caused needless confusion.

grounding: Shows a worker stung and lost after a vague 'not good enough', until she asks for specifics.

passage:
Sonali: "Avni, I read your presentation. It's not there yet."
Avni: "Okay. What's missing?"
Sonali: "It just doesn't feel strong."
Avni: "Is it the data? The slides? The story?"
Sonali: "Hard to say. It needs more punch."
Avni: "More punch where? The opening?"
Sonali: "Just... overall. You'll figure it out."
(Sonali walks off. Avni stares at the twenty slides.)
Avni: (to herself) "Figure out what?"
(Later, to her friend on the phone.)
Avni: "I've changed the colours, the fonts, the order. I have no idea if it's better. I feel like I failed a test nobody told me the questions to."

qa.q: How many slides were in Avni's presentation?
qa.a: Avni stared at the twenty slides.

qa.q: How did Avni feel after Sonali walked off?
qa.a: She felt hurt, confused and helpless, as if she had failed a test with unknown questions.

qa.q: What could Sonali have said instead?
qa.a: Sonali could point to one specific slide, say what works, what needs to change and why, so Avni could act.

qa.q: How might Sonali see those comments?
qa.a: Sonali probably thinks the feedback was honest, not noticing that without specifics it gives Avni nothing to use.

grounding: A dialogue shows a worker receiving vague feedback like 'needs more punch' and feeling both stung and lost.

passage: I'm Mahima, and my first performance review still makes me wince. My manager, Manoj, read from a sheet: "Communication needs improvement. Attitude could be better. Not meeting expectations." I asked for an example. He said, "You know what I mean." I didn't. I went through my emails that night, trying to find the rude one. I couldn't. For weeks I spoke less in meetings, scared of saying something wrong. It wasn't until a senior colleague sat with me that I learned the real issue: I'd sent a client report without copying Manoj. One email. That was fixable in a second. The vague words had just hurt, and taught me nothing.

qa.q: What did Mahima turn out to have done?
qa.a: Mahima had sent a client report without copying Manoj.

qa.q: How did Mahima feel in the weeks after the review?
qa.a: Mahima felt hurt and scared, speaking less in meetings for fear of saying something wrong.

qa.q: What would have made Manoj's feedback useful?
qa.a: Naming the specific email and why it mattered, so Mahima could fix it straight away.

qa.q: How might the senior colleague's help have felt to Mahima?
qa.a: It likely felt a huge relief, finally turning the vague criticism into one small, fixable problem.

grounding: A worker recalls vague, harsh review comments that stung and taught nothing until someone named the specific issue.

passage:
Training coordinator's note, Wednesday, design studio.
At the eleven o'clock review, Dhruv flipped through Tejas's façade drawings for the school project in under a minute, said "Not good enough. Redo it," and moved to the next desk. No example, no mark on the sheets. Tejas said "Okay" very quietly. For the next hour I watched him open and close the same file, change a window size, change it back. At lunch he didn't eat. When I asked how it was going, he said, "I don't even know what's wrong. The windows? The colour? Me?" His voice cracked on the last word.
What I did: I asked Dhruv for three specific points before evening. Dhruv wrote them down: the entrance is hard to find, the sunshades face the wrong way, the front is too busy. I sat with Tejas while he read them. He nodded slowly. "I can fix those."

qa.q: How long did Dhruv spend on Tejas's drawings at the review?
qa.a: Under a minute.

qa.q: How was Tejas feeling after the review?
qa.a: He felt stung and lost, unsure what was wrong and even wondering if the problem was him; his voice cracked and he skipped lunch.

qa.q: What did the coordinator's step do that the review did not?
qa.a: Asking Dhruv for three specific points turned a hurtful verdict into things Tejas could act on: the entrance, the sunshades and the busy front.

qa.q: How might Dhruv have seen that one-minute review?
qa.a: Dhruv was probably rushing between desks and may have thought "not good enough" was clear, without noticing it told Tejas nothing and hurt a lot.

grounding: Shows a young worker given "not good enough" with no example, left both hurt and lost until specific points arrive.
